personas.role: Runs the resource server: prices routes, answers 402, and asks a facilitator to verify and settle.
goals: Charge per call without accounts or invoices
Get paid in the same request that serves the data
Keep chain work out of the API team's code
pains: Picking a facilitator for production because the x402.org default serves testnets only
Handler work that is lost when a settle fails under the authorization flow
Timeouts on /settle that leave the outcome unknown
implements: Payment middleware such as @x402/express with a route map of accepts entries
An x402ResourceServer wired to an HTTPFacilitatorClient
mustTrust: The facilitator to verify honestly and broadcast promptly
The asset contract to enforce the nonce and the window
Its own route matching (past releases fixed encoded-path bypasses)
questions: Which facilitator supports my network and scheme, and what does it charge?
Do I need exact, upto or auth-capture for this endpoint?
What happens to my handler output if the settle fails?
firstSteps: Run the @x402/express quick start against Base Sepolia with the x402.org facilitator
Price one route at $0.01 and watch the PAYMENT-REQUIRED header
Choose a production facilitator and compare its fees and networks
personas.story: Maya runs a weather API that used to sell monthly keys. She adds the Express middleware, prices the forecast route at one cent in USDC on Base, and points it at a facilitator. The first agent request gets a 402 with the price in a header; the retry carries a signature, the facilitator says it is valid, her handler runs, and the settle returns a transaction hash. On Friday a facilitator outage turns into a burst of 502 answers, and two settles time out. She checks both hashes on chain before retrying, finds one already confirmed, and writes a small reconciliation job so it never needs a person again.

personas.role: Builds the client side: an agent or app that meets 402 responses, chooses an option, signs and retries.
goals: Let an agent pay for data and tools without a sign-up per vendor
Keep the agent inside a budget
pains: Two wire formats (V1 and V2) in the wild
Deciding which accepts entry to pick across networks and assets
Spending limits that exist only in the SDK, not in the protocol
implements: wrapFetchWithPaymentFromConfig from @x402/fetch with a registered scheme
mustTrust: The server's PAYMENT-REQUIRED header, especially payTo
The server to deliver after a settle
questions: Is this server on V1 or V2?
What cap should my agent have per payment and per day?
Can I get a refund if the response is useless?
firstSteps: Wrap fetch with @x402/fetch and call a testnet endpoint
Set spendControls to a cap below $1 and test a refusal
Log every PAYMENT-RESPONSE hash with the request it paid for
metrics: Latency added by the 402 round trip
personas.story: Dev builds a research agent that buys market data from five APIs. He wraps fetch with the x402 client and registers the exact EVM scheme for Base. The SDK already refuses unknown assets and anything above $1, so he lowers the cap to ten cents and adds a policy that skips Solana entries for now. One API still speaks V1 and answers with a JSON body; he registers the V1 client for that host. Every PAYMENT-RESPONSE hash goes into the task log next to the URL. When one provider returns empty data after payment, he finds there is no refund path under exact and moves that provider to a manual allowlist.

personas.role: Operates the verify and settle service, pays gas, and publishes what it supports.
goals: Verify fast and settle reliably across networks
Recover gas and costs through fees
pains: Duplicate settlement races and Solana duplicate submissions
Keeping signer keys funded for gas
Sanctions screening and its legal exposure
implements: Nonce and replay checks, simulation and settlement caches
KYT and OFAC screening where it chooses to offer it
mustTrust: Resource servers to send their own requirements, not the client's echo
questions: Which schemes and networks do I list in /supported?
How do I make /settle idempotent across processes?
What do I return when a receipt never arrives?
firstSteps: Run a self-facilitation example against a testnet
Implement the eight facilitator safety rules from the security literature
Publish /supported with signers per CAIP-2 family
personas.story: Priya runs a facilitator for three EVM chains and Solana. Her /supported answer lists exact and upto on each chain and one signer per family. Most of her day is not cryptography but operations: keeping the gas wallets topped up, watching the share of settles that end as settlement_pending, and making sure a retried settle from a second worker cannot broadcast twice. A paper on facilitator safety rules lands, and she maps each rule to a test. Screening runs before every settle; when a payer address matches a sanctions list, the settle fails with a clear reason and the resource server returns 402 instead of the data.

personas.role: Pays on its own within limits a human set, choosing among accepts entries per request.
goals: Pay only for what the task needs
pains: Servers that take payment and return nothing useful
Altered 402 responses that name another payTo
mustTrust: The facilitator not to stall payments
questions: Is this payTo the seller I meant to pay?
Is the price within my cap?
Do I have a way back if the result is wrong?
firstSteps: Check payTo against the expected seller before every signature
Refuse amounts above the configured cap
Record each transaction hash with the task step
personas.story: The agent is asked to compile a report from paid sources overnight. Each fetch that returns 402 goes through the same checks: the network and asset are on its list, the amount is under five cents, and the payTo matches the address its operator pinned for that domain. One source suddenly asks for twenty cents; the agent refuses and notes it. Another returns a 402 whose payTo differs from the pinned one, so it stops and flags the domain. By morning it has spent a little over a dollar across ninety calls, and every payment in its log has a transaction hash a human can check.

personas.role: Decides whether and how the business may accept or send x402 payments, and what screening and records it needs.
goals: Know who handles sanctions screening and travel-rule data
pains: The protocol has no KYC, know-your-agent or sanctions layer
Payment metadata can contain personal data sent to third parties
Volume figures that cannot be relied on
implements: Record keeping of PAYMENT-RESPONSE hashes and offers or receipts
mustTrust: The facilitator's screening and its records
Product terms such as Cloudflare's merchant-of-record role in cloudflare:402
questions: Is our facilitator a money transmitter in our markets?
Who is merchant of record in each variant we use?
What personal data leaves our systems in resource descriptions?
firstSteps: Map which facilitator screens what (the CDP facilitator runs OFAC and KYT checks)
Review section J for each market we sell in
Strip personal data from resource URLs and descriptions
personas.story: Lena reviews the plan to sell API calls through x402 in the US and the EU. The first thing she notices is what the protocol leaves out: no identity, no sanctions check, no dispute process. Screening therefore depends on the facilitator, and the team's chosen facilitator documents OFAC and KYT checks on every payment, which she records as a vendor control. She asks the engineers to stop putting customer names in resource descriptions, because those travel to the facilitator. For the credit-backed Cloudflare variant she notes that Cloudflare is merchant of record with its own terms, and she sends that contract to legal.

personas.role: Builds independent controls around x402: budgets, allowlists, approvals and monitoring at the client, edge or facilitator.
goals: Enforce limits the protocol does not define
pains: Budgets are out of scope in the spec
On chain, x402 payments look like ordinary transfers
implements: Policies and hooks such as onBeforePaymentCreation and onBeforeSettle
Monitoring on facilitator events and contract events
mustTrust: The SDK to call its hooks in order
The facilitator to report outcomes accurately
questions: Where can I stop a payment: before signing, at the edge, or at settle?
How do I tell x402 payments from other transfers?
Can I revoke a signed authorization before it settles?
firstSteps: Add a policy that enforces a payTo allowlist before signing
Set validBefore windows as short as the use allows
Subscribe to settle outcomes and alert on unusual spend
metrics: Coverage of agents under a policy
personas.story: Omar's team sells a spend-control layer to companies that run agents. For x402 his main lever is the client: a policy hook that runs before the payment is created, checks payTo against an allowlist, enforces a daily budget per agent, and refuses unknown assets. A second lever is short validity windows, because a signed authorization cannot be recalled once it leaves the agent. On the seller side he offers hooks before verify and settle. Monitoring is harder: on chain the payments look like ordinary token transfers, so he relies on the facilitator's records and builder codes where sellers use them.

rows.step: Enforce spend caps and payTo allowlists
Settle on chain and pay gas (POST /settle)
Return and store the PAYMENT-RESPONSE receipt
